newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil poised to take advantage of S&P upgrade.
newsitem.headline: Brazil poised to take advantage of S&P upgrade.

text.p: Brazil appeared ready to take advantage of a fresh credit upgrade from Standard & Poor's Corp, having recently cleared the way to issue $5 billion in Yankee bonds and begun testing waters in Europe's parallel bond market.
Although the sovereign was not expected to issue debt before its 500 billion lire deal scheduled for May, officials said they were preparing the groundwork to tap new markets.

"We have no plans now other than the Italian lira deal. We just want to be ready to take advantage of good market conditions when they arise," Central Bank adviser Marcio Cartier Marques told Reuters.
Analysts said the government's effort will be aided by Standard & Poor's decision on Wednesday to upgrade Brazil's long-term foreign currency rating to BB-minus from B-plus.

The upgrade, which S&P said was based on increasing political support for the government's fiscal reform drive, was seen as confirmation of a growing perception in the market that Brazil risk was on the mend.

Brazilian debt prices did not move substantially higher on S&P's upgrade. But analysts said that in the short- to medium-term, the change would benefit the republic and corporates in the form of cheaper borrowing costs.
The Central Bank's foreign borrowing strategy to date has been to issue debt in a variety of currencies to set benchmarks and open new markets for corporate issuers.
With plenty of Brazilian paper in a variety of currencies alredy in the Eurobond market, officials are turning to other markets and different types of issues.

The Central Bank's Cartier said that earlier this week, Brazil began asking banks to prepare proposals to issue Eurobonds in several European currencies which would be fungible, or redenominated, to the euro after the introduction of the single European currency in 1999.
The issues are called "parallel bonds" because they carry the same maturity and coupon in a variety of currencies.
Although parallel bonds have been issued by a number of European countries, a Brazilian deal could carry some novelty value.

"No Latin American country or emerging market nation has done a parallel bond yet," Cartier said. He added that it was not Brazil's primary intention to be the first parallel bond issuer but rather to establish a presence in a market that is bound to become more popular in the countdown to 1999.
Cartier refused to give an idea when the parallel deal would be priced. Market sources said Brazil would probably wait until after its lira deal.

In addition to the parallel bond market, Brazil is also eyeing the Yankee bond market. Last week it filed a shelf registration with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to issue up to $5 billion in debt.
Federally owned Telebras has already announced plans to issue a $300 million Yankee bond sometime in the second quarter.
